chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading Trade War Signals as an Investor

lessons.title: Tracking Tariff Announcements and Policy Signals Before They Hit Your Portfolio

children.text: Chapters 1 and 2 explained what already happened. This chapter is about what you do next time, before the headline finishes trending. That means knowing exactly where tariff decisions actually get announced, which market indicators move first, and how to read a company's own commentary before the sector story reaches the front page.
Primary Sources: Where Tariff Decisions Actually Get Announced

Every tariff you will ever trade around was first published somewhere official, days or weeks before it became a headline you noticed. Skipping straight to news aggregators means you are reading a summary of a summary.

cards.definition: The Office of the US Trade Representative. Publishes the actual Section 301 tariff lists, exclusion processes, and negotiation updates for US trade actions, including anything affecting India.

India's Directorate General of Foreign Trade, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Publishes India's own export/import policy notifications, including any retaliatory measures or export incentive changes.
The US government's official daily journal, where a tariff order becomes legally binding once published, often with the exact effective date and product HS codes.

Where countries formally challenge each other's trade measures. A new WTO complaint filed against a tariff is a signal that diplomatic channels have not resolved it, though WTO rulings themselves can take years.

body.label: USTR Press Releases
body.description: The primary source for US Section 301 and Section 232 tariff announcements, exclusion requests, and negotiation updates.

body.label: DGFT Notifications
body.description: India's own export/import policy notifications, including any measures taken in response to a foreign tariff action.

children.text: The three transmission channels from Chapter 2, currency, commodities, and capital flows, are also your monitoring dashboard. They tend to move before the Nifty fully reprices, because currency and commodity markets trade around the clock and react to policy signals faster than equity markets can digest them.

body.caption: Market Signals and What They're Telling You

cells: Rising sharply usually means global risk-off, with rupee pressure to follow
Any major financial data website or terminal
Rising means the market is pricing higher near-term volatility
NSE website, or your broker's platform (e.g. Zerodha Kite)
Widening means the market is pricing in more rupee depreciation risk ahead, not just today's spot move
Bank and broker FX desks, RBI publications
Sharp moves reflect both global growth fear and oil-specific supply and demand, check which one is driving it
MCX, ICE, or standard financial news feeds

children.text: Company-Level Signals: Concalls and Trade Data

markDefs.definition: The post-results conference call Indian listed companies hold with analysts and investors, discussing quarterly performance and forward guidance. Transcripts are published and are one of the most underused primary sources available to retail investors.

children.text: Two Indian-specific sources are genuinely underused. First, quarterly earnings

, management teams at export-facing companies are usually asked directly about tariff exposure, and their answers, hedged or specific, are a better read on company-level risk than any analyst's sector note. Second, GSTN's monthly e-way bill generation data is a genuine high-frequency proxy for goods movement across the economy; a sustained slowdown in e-way bill volumes for export-linked states or sectors can show up in the data before it shows up in quarterly results.

body.label: screener.in - Concall Transcripts
body.description: Screener.in aggregates concall transcripts and investor presentations for most listed Indian companies in one place, useful for reading management's own words on tariff exposure rather than a paraphrased summary.

body.title: Read the Concall
body.scenario: In a hypothetical quarterly concall, an analyst asks a garment exporter's management about US tariff exposure. Management responds: "We've already begun requalifying two customers who were sourcing from us for their US-bound orders. We expect some near-term order deferrals this quarter, but we've also opened conversations with three new EU-based buyers who are looking to diversify their own sourcing."
body.prompt: Is this management team signaling rising risk, falling risk, or something more specific? What would you want to ask as a follow-up?
body.modelAnswer: It is a mixed signal, not simply rising or falling risk, and that specificity is exactly why concalls beat headlines. There is near-term pain acknowledged directly (order deferrals this quarter from US-bound business), but also an adaptive response already in motion (new EU buyers). A useful follow-up would be asking what share of revenue the affected US orders represented, and over what timeline the EU pipeline could realistically offset it, since "we've opened conversations" is a much earlier stage than a signed order book.

children.text: Reading the Retaliation Pattern, Not Just the Headline

You already learned in Chapter 1 that a trade war is defined by the retaliation cycle, not any single move. That distinction shows up in the language official statements actually use. Escalation language tends to include phrases like "in response to," "further measures if," and specific new HS codes or product lists. De-escalation language tends to include "exemption process," "productive discussions," "temporary suspension," or a specific date set for renewed talks. Reading the actual statement, not the headline written about it, is often the fastest way to tell which direction things are heading.

body.title: A Weekly Monitoring Routine
steps: Daily: scan DXY, India VIX, and USD/INR for unusual moves, not the absolute level, the size of the move relative to a normal day
Weekly: check USTR and DGFT notification pages for any new filings affecting sectors you hold
Around results season: read concall transcripts for export-facing holdings directly, don't rely only on the earnings summary
Monthly: glance at GSTN e-way bill data trends if you are tracking export-linked sectors specifically
Whenever a new headline breaks: find the actual official statement or notification before adjusting any position based on the headline alone

body.text: Unverified leaks and "sources say" reports move fast and are wrong often enough to be dangerous. Confirm any major tariff development against a primary source, USTR, DGFT, or the Federal Register, before treating it as confirmed enough to act on. Trading on a rumor that turns out to be false is a self-inflicted version of the very volatility this course is trying to help you read.

The investors who read a trade war well are not the ones who react fastest to headlines. They are the ones who already know where the primary source is, what the market's early-warning indicators look like on a normal day, and what a company's own management is actually saying, so a headline just confirms what they were already watching.

points: Every tariff exists as an official notification, USTR, DGFT, or the Federal Register, before it becomes a headline; read the primary source, not the summary of the summary.
DXY, India VIX, USD/INR forward premiums, and Brent crude are your early-warning dashboard, built directly from the three transmission channels in Chapter 2.
Earnings concalls and GSTN e-way bill data are underused, India-specific sources that often show company- and sector-level stress before it appears in quarterly results.

Escalation language ("in response to," "further measures if") and de-escalation language ("exemption process," "productive discussions") in official statements are a faster tell than most news headlines.
Never act on an unverified report. Confirm against a primary source first.
